<note>the text continues the discussion of life-force virtues</note> similar things happen: thus they report that in cases of colic <note>original: "torminibus"; severe abdominal pain</note>, if a live duck is applied to the belly, the disease passes away and the duck dies. It is a similar thing which Archytas <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician</note> says: if a heart recently extracted from an animal, while still warm and living, is suspended over a patient with a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>, it cures it. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a Hoopoe, or a Swallow, or a Weasel, or a Mole, while it is still living and palpitating, it confers upon him memory, recollection, intellect, and divination. 

From this has arisen a general precept: that whatever things are to be collected from animals—whether stones, members, or excrements such as hair, dung, or claws—these ought to be taken from the animals while they are still living, and also, if it can be done, with the animals themselves remaining alive afterward. Hence they instruct that when you collect the tongue of a Frog, you should return it alive to the water; if you collect a tooth or an eye of a Wolf, you should not kill the Wolf; and so with similar things. 

Thus Democritus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher, often cited in occult literature for natural magic</note> reports that if anyone extracts the tongue of a living Sea-frog <note>original: "Ranæ marinæ"; likely referring to the Anglerfish or a similar creature</note> without any other part of the body adhering to it, and after the creature is let back into the sea, he places the tongue over the heart-palpitation of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever he asks. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, tied to a sick person before sunrise in such a way that the frogs are released blind into the water, drive away tertian fevers <note>A fever recurring every third day</note>. They also report that these same eyes, tied in a deer skin along with the flesh of a Nightingale, produce wakefulness and put sleep to flight. Similarly, the spine <note>original: "radius"; literally a ray or sting</note> of a Stingray <note>original: "Pastinacæ"</note> tied to the navel is said to make births easy.

<summary>This page describes sympathetic magic and medical remedies involving the use of living animal parts. It emphasizes that certain magical virtues are most potent when the organ is harvested from a living creature that survives the process.</summary>
<keywords>sympathetic magic, Archytas, animal hearts, Democritus, divination, folk medicine, quartan fever, stingray, nightingale, frog tongue</keywords>
